item.title: Branch-Extended Automatic Differentiation
item.description: arXiv:2611.08637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present branch-extended automatic differentiation (BEAD), a software package that provides information about inactive branches of piecewise-differentiable functions, intended for use in nonsmooth optimization algorithms. BEAD is implemented in Python, building on the popular JAX framework. For supported nonsmooth operations such as abs and max, BEAD identifies alternative branches within tolerance from the given input, and computes gradients of the resulting branches extended to the given input. Such information has been previously used for robust optimization methods, but has required error-prone and tedious manual differentiation, unlike BEAD, which is fully automated for functions written in NumPy-like JAX code. Our experiments show that our approach is as accurate as manually written derivative code, and offers more flexibility in modifying the function and choosing between branch-discovery rules. While we were originally motivated by the manifold sampling algorithm for nonsmooth composite objectives, we also integrate BEAD branch-extension gradients into a nonsmooth BFGS-SQP solver. On two small nonsmooth test problems, the resulting path-aware search resolves failures or substantially reduces the number of evaluations required by the BFGS-SQP solver.
item.dc:creator: Jan H\"uckelheim, Jeffrey Larson, Matt Menickelly

item.title: Compressed Per-Player Local Methods for Multiplayer Federated Learning: Exact Convergence via Increment Sharing
item.description: arXiv:2611.08686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL), introduced by Yoon et al. (2025), extends classical federated learning to settings where clients are rational players in a game with individual objectives and strategies, seeking an equilibrium. A natural baseline is Per-Player Local SGD (PEARL-SGD), where each player performs several local SGD steps before exchanging strategies through a central server. However, the original PEARL-SGD formulation does not extend cleanly to compressed communication. Directly compressing the players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium, even with deterministic gradients. To address this issue, we reformulate PEARL-SGD so that players communicate local strategy increments rather than the strategies themselves. Without compression, the two formulations are equivalent, but with compression, increment sharing preserves exact convergence, allowing us to design the communication-efficient compressed PEARL-SGD (C-PEARL-SGD). Beyond compression, we also consider variance reduction as another axis of improvement, introducing PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG. Under the original MpFL assumptions, we establish convergence guarantees for all variants through a unified parametric inequality. Numerical experiments, including distributed spectrum sensing, demonstrate the practical benefits of our methods over vanilla PEARL-SGD.
item.dc:creator: Bhavika Balani, TaeHo Yoon, Nicolas Loizou

item.title: Optimal Feedback Control of the Fokker-Planck Equation for an SIRS Epidemic Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.08708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a Fokker--Planck feedback control framework for a stochastic susceptible--infected--recovered--susceptible (SIRS) epidemic model with three intervention mechanisms targeting disease transmission, loss of immunity, and recovery. The interventions are formulated as space- and time-dependent feedback controls that influence both the drift and diffusion coefficients of the underlying stochastic differential equations, allowing control of the probability distribution of epidemic states. We investigate the existence of optimal controls and derive first-order necessary optimality conditions involving a forward Fokker--Planck equation, a backward adjoint equation, and a Hamiltonian minimization condition. For numerical approximation, we combine a Chang--Cooper discretization of the diagonal drift--diffusion terms with a finite-difference treatment of cross-diffusion and a sequential quadratic Hamiltonian (SQH) algorithm for computing the optimal feedback policies. We also examine sufficient-decrease and convergence properties of the SQH iteration. Numerical experiments consider four epidemiological objectives involving cumulative infection burden, infection-threshold exceedance, terminal susceptible population, and a combination of running and terminal costs. The resulting feedback policies exhibit distinct spatial and temporal structures depending on the epidemiological objective. Monte Carlo simulations of the underlying stochastic system illustrate that the optimized interventions can substantially reduce infection growth and undesirable epidemic outcomes relative to uncontrolled dynamics. The proposed framework provides a distribution-based approach to stochastic epidemic control that integrates mathematical analysis, numerical optimization, and state-dependent intervention design.
item.dc:creator: Christian Parkinson, Souvik Roy

item.title: Vector Lyapunov functions for nonconvex constrained optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.08729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonconvex constrained optimization problems are commonly solved by a Newton method for necessary conditions (sequential linear/quadratic programming) or a barrier reformulation (interior-point methods). We present a vector Lyapunov analysis for Newton-type algorithms based on constraint violation and optimality of the primal solutions to a sequence of approximate optimization problems. We thus prove local stability and convergence by constructing a strict Lyapunov function for the primal solution.
item.dc:creator: Torbj{\o}rn Cunis, Ilya Kolmanovsky

item.title: Constrained Nested-Logit Pricing: An Exact Reformulation and Global Optimization Method
item.description: arXiv:2611.09023v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sellers must price substitutable products while meeting operational requirements such as price limits and sales targets. Nested logit captures stronger substitution among similar products, but these requirements can undermine the structure used to solve unconstrained pricing problems. We develop an exact reformulation and a global optimization method for a fixed assortment with price bounds and weighted price caps. The key novelty is to concentrate the difficult interactions at the nest level while retaining convex optimization over individual products, without discretizing prices or approximating demand. This structure makes the number of nests, rather than products, govern the exponent in a conditional worst-case complexity bound. The method returns feasible prices together with a bound on how much profit could still be gained, allowing decision makers to assess solution quality even when computation stops early. Extensions cover purchase-probability bounds and price-order rules, with explicit accounts of their computational cost. In synthetic experiments, the method certifies solutions for assortments of up to 500 products with few nests. Projecting unconstrained prices onto the feasible set loses up to 32.60% of profit relative to direct constrained optimization, highlighting the value of jointly optimizing substitution and feasibility.
item.dc:creator: Hoang Giang Pham, Tien Mai

item.title: Resolvent-Diagonal Energy of Isospectral Jacobi Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2611.09050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the minimum squared resolvent diagonal among Jacobi matrices with prescribed eigenvalues. For the zeros of $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}$, we construct a canonical realization and bound its asymptotic cost against the optimum. Its rescaled inverse converges to the Green operator of a reflection-symmetric singular Schr\"odinger operator with Bessel-zero spectrum. A Green-coordinate identity places this construction and all finite realizations in the same density framework. Mass-constrained spectral problems then give computable lower bounds. The bounds meet at $\alpha=1/2$, with optimal energy $2/15$, and have first-order contact with derivative $-13/75$. We classify the constrained extremal profiles and the three endpoint geometries of the canonical density. Two polynomial families with the same limiting edge spectrum have different limiting optimal energies. For Nesterov momentum $(s-1)/(s+1)$, the optimal leading endpoint Hessian-drift gain among nonnegative-link Jacobi realizations is $\sqrt{2}$ times the original gain. An explicit isospectral flow strictly improves the standard one-sided realization for $\alpha>-1/2$, $\alpha\ne1/2$.
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}

item.title: A Smooth Equality Reformulation of Nonlinear Exponential Cone Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exponential cone optimization has received considerable attention in the modern literature, but studies involving nonlinear objective and constraint functions are still limited. This work can be seen as one of the first steps toward understanding nonlinear exponential cone optimization (NECO) problems. Here, we ask the question "Can smooth equality constraints replace nonlinear exponential cone constraints?". From a practical point of view, even squared slack reformulations in nonlinear programming introduce difficulties. However, such reformulations can be useful for studying optimality conditions. Motivated by this observation, in this work, we use a smooth surjective parameterization of the exponential cone to reformulate NECO as an equality-constrained nonlinear program (RNLP). We then analyze Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) and second-order optimality conditions for NECO through RNLP. Although feasibility is represented exactly, the KKT conditions for RNLP do not in general guarantee those for NECO. We characterize this correspondence through multiplier restrictions that are equivalent to a second-order condition involving only slack variables. We also establish an exact curvature identity showing that RNLP reproduces the sigma term of NECO without additional assumptions. Finally, we prove the relationships between second-order necessary and sufficient conditions for the two problems. We identify when RNLP can be used to rule out local minimizers of NECO or establish strict local optimality for NECO without explicitly evaluating the sigma term.
item.dc:creator: Huimin Li, Ellen H. Fukuda

item.title: Second-order optimality conditions for $C^{1,1}$ sparsity constrained optimization problems via disjunctive programming
item.description: arXiv:2611.09146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate second-order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for a class of $C^{1,1}$ sparsity constrained optimization problems via a disjunctive programming approach. More precisely, by utilizing the limiting/Mordukhovich second-order subdifferential of the associated Lagrangian function, we establish new second-order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for local optimal solutions. These results are derived under mild assumptions and extend several existing results in the literature. In addition, we apply our theoretical developments to sparse multiobjective optimization problems and derive second-order optimality conditions for efficient solutions.
item.dc:creator: Luu Thi Thu Huyen, Liguo Jiao, Nguyen Van Tuyen

item.title: The multiplier step size in classical two-block ADMM: convergence and counterexamples
item.description: arXiv:2611.09169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How large can the multiplier step be in the classical two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)? We keep the penalty fixed and use the usual primal updates. We consider finite-dimensional problems with closed proper convex objectives. We assume that a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker point exists and that each block subproblem attains its minimum at every step. Under these assumptions, the constraint images and the multiplier converge for a range of factors that extends beyond the golden ratio. The constraint matrices may be rank deficient. For larger steps, we construct two fixed compact polytopes and give an explicit threshold below two. The polytopes admit an infeasible periodic orbit for every factor at or above this threshold. At that threshold, ADMM can cycle even for smooth strongly convex objectives. This gives a negative answer to Glowinski's question about the full interval from zero to two. A different pair of piecewise-quadratic objectives gives geometrically growing residuals. For the general convex class, we locate the endpoint of the uniform convergence interval near 1.88688256. A convergence certificate on the unit circle gives the lower bound, while a separate periodic orbit gives the upper bound. Exact arithmetic verifies that the two bounds differ by less than 0.000000174.
item.dc:creator: Benqi Liu, Qiming Dai, Zaiwen Wen

item.title: Real-Time Nonlinear Mixed-Integer Model Predictive Control With Horizon-Tail Relaxations
item.description: arXiv:2611.09187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) of nonlinear systems with discrete decisions leads to mixed-integer nonlinear programs (MINLPs) whose combinatorial complexity often prevents real-time deployment. In this paper, we propose a decomposition-based MPC method that reorders and reduces computations to shorten the delay between receiving a state measurement and applying the control input. Before the measurement arrives, we solve a continuous relaxation of the MINLP at a predicted state and construct a mixed-integer quadratic program (MIQP). Once the measured state is available, we solve the MIQP that reconstructs the discrete controls and simultaneously performs one sequential quadratic programming step toward the corresponding nonlinear solution. To reduce the combinatorial complexity in the horizon length, we either fix the integer controls or relax their integrality over the prediction horizon tail, while retaining an integer-feasible first control input. We derive error bounds relating the nonlinear objective values obtained with the horizon-tail approximations to the optimal value of the original mixed-integer problem. In a data center cooling example, the proposed method reduces mean feedback computation time by 94% relative to a state-of-the-art MINLP method with a total closed-loop cost difference of less than 1%.
item.dc:creator: Armin Nurkanovi\'c

item.title: Tracking of a Moving Target on a Hyperboloid and its Extension to Leader-follower Formation Controller
item.description: arXiv:2611.09261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a novel controller for a double-integrator agent to track a moving target with bounded velocity on a hyperboloid $\mathbb{H}^n$. The control law uses the intrinsic Riemannian structure of the hyperboloid, including the logarithm map, covariant derivative, and parallel transport, to make all its terms coordinate-free. Such formulation eases the implementation of the proposed tracking controller in the ambient Minkowski space without doing any additional chart computations. We use Barbalat's lemma for the hyperboloid to establish the convergence proof. Later, the proposed tracking controller is extended to a leader-follower formation control, where each agent reaches at a desired position around a moving leader in $\mathbb{H}^n$. We validate the results with numerical simulations considering two different target trajectories, geodesic and spiral, as examples.
item.dc:creator: Ashish Shukla, Sanad Shaha, Kashyap Rajeevsarathy, Arijit Sen

item.title: Hierarchical Signal Temporal Logic Control of Continuous-Time Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.09283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For linear continuous-time systems, we solve the signal temporal logic (STL) control problem by translating it from continuous to discrete time such that a solution to the discrete-time problem guarantees a solution to the original continuous-time one. We split control synthesis into three hierarchical tasks. First, we discretize the continuous-time STL formula into a discrete-time one by sampling the temporal behavior it specifies. We accordingly discretize the continuous-time system by constructing a discrete-time model such that the input-state trajectories of the continuous-time system can be characterized as piecewise polynomial interpolations of the input-state trajectories of the discrete-time model. Second, we exploit this characterization to formulate mixed-integer linear constraints on the discrete-time trajectories that allow for planning a trajectory whose piecewise polynomial interpolation satisfies the continuous-time STL formula. In fact, system discretization and trajectory planning are performed in such a manner that any feasible solution to these constraints gives a discrete-time trajectory that can be transformed into a continuous-time one guaranteed to satisfy the original STL formula. Third, we propose a step-by-step algorithm to construct the control input that realizes such continuous-time trajectory.
item.dc:creator: Armin Pirastehzad, Bart Besselink

item.title: PH-Symb : Sparse symbolic identification of nonlinear port-Hamiltoniansystems using Kolmogorov-Arnold networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.09334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper introduces PH-Symb, a novel symbolic structure-preserving identification method, that combines Kolmogorov Arnold networks and sparse regression to build explicit port-Hamiltonian (pH) models from data. Unlike other Machine Learning or neural pH approaches, PH-Symb recovers physically interpretable and explicit-symbolic components and enforces pH structure by construction. It also introduces a new normalization method that preserves the pH structure. It allows handling both identification from input-state-output (ISO) data and input-output (IO) data, and applications show it delivers interpretable models and lower errors than neural baselines on synthetic and real-world systems.
item.dc:creator: Achraf El Messaoudi (Umlp, Supmicrotech - Ensmm, Femto-St), Karim Cherifi (Umlp, Supmicrotech - Ensmm, Femto-St), Yann Le Gorrec (Umlp, Supmicrotech - Ensmm, Femto-St), Yongxin Wu (Umlp, Supmicrotech - Ensmm, Femto-St)

item.title: Approximation Algorithms for Right-Hand-Side Parametric Linear Programming Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.09378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In parametric linear optimization problems, the objective function or the feasible set depends linearly on one or several real-valued parameters. The goal is to provide an optimal solution set, i.e., a set containing an optimal solution for each non-parametric problem induced by a particular choice of parameter values. In this paper, we consider right-hand-side single-parametric linear programming problems (RHS-PLPPs) that are usually very difficult to solve exactly. An optimal solution set of minimum cardinality can be infinite, while a representation by optimal bases may still require super-polynomially many different bases. Hence, we develop approximation methods for RHS-PLPPs that compute approximation sets of polynomially bounded cardinality, each containing, for every parameter value, a feasible solution whose objective value is at most a prescribed multiplicative factor times the optimum. Our first approach constructs an approximation set using a greedy staircase procedure and yields an FPTAS under general sufficient conditions. We show that these conditions hold for some important classes of RHS-PLPPs. For monotone instances, in which the feasible sets are nested as the parameter varies, our algorithm yields an approximation set of minimum cardinality. Beyond monotonicity, we establish near-minimum cardinality guarantees under more general sufficient conditions. Finally, we introduce a dual approximation algorithm that returns solutions with objective value no greater than the optimum while allowing a controlled multiplicative violation of the parameter-dependent right-hand sides.
item.dc:creator: Levin Nemesch, Stefan Ruzika, Clemens Thielen, Alina Wittmann

item.title: Data-driven representation of continuous-time linear time-invariant behaviors via Hankel integral operators
item.description: arXiv:2611.09530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a data-driven representation of the finite-horizon behavior of deterministic controllable continuous-time LTI systems. We first introduce a notion of persistency of excitation for continuous-time signals that does not require the signal to be differentiable. We then show that, when the input is persistently exciting in this sense, the closure of the range of a Hankel integral operator built from a single input-output trajectory equals the behavior of the system over a finite time horizon. This result provides a nonparametric representation of system trajectories directly in terms of measured data, without requiring an explicit parametric model of the system.
item.dc:creator: Fritz A. Engeln, Marta Zag\'orowska, Jan-Willem van Wingerden

item.title: Can a Language Model Write the Weights? An Empirical Study of LLM-Written Scoring Networks for Column Generation and MILP Branching, with a Bus-Driver Scheduling Application
item.description: arXiv:2611.09559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper was generated by an AI model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) under the author's direction; all results come from computations run on the author's machine, and every reference was checked. Weight-space programming (WSP) is the idea that a large language model (LLM) can write the weights of a small neural network directly, guided only by reading forward-pass outputs, with no gradient training. We test whether WSP can improve exact operations research algorithms where they rely on cheap scoring rules. In four studies, an LLM wrote small multilayer perceptrons that (i) select arcs, labels and ng-neighbourhoods inside column generation for the vehicle routing problem with time windows, and (ii) choose branching variables in SCIP's branch-and-bound. The algorithms stay exact whatever the weights; a bad network only costs time. In column generation, no lever gave a material gain. In branching on synthetic classes, a hand-written network solved independent-set instances in 0.37x the time of SCIP's default rule (18 paired instances, Wilcoxon $p<10^{-5}$) and matched or beat networks trained by imitation of strong branching, but on 39 MIPLIB 2017 instances it solved 19 versus 24. In an application built from the real GTFS feed of Atlanta's transit agency (MARTA), a crew scheduling set-partitioning model solved by a native C plugin with SCIP's factory settings, the LLM-written rules took 0.63x the default's time on 32 held-out instances ($p<10^{-4}$), but SCIP's plain pseudocost rule did exactly as well (ratio 0.99, $p=0.19$). In these settings, the gains came from being cheap, not from what the LLM wrote. All code, logs and the numbers behind every figure are released.
item.dc:creator: Renan Butkeraites

item.title: A Regular First-Order Calculus for the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.09691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a notion of intrinsic differentiability for functionals on the space of finite nonnegative measures equipped with the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao (WFR) distance, also known as the Hellinger--Kantorovich (HK) distance. The resulting static first-order calculus accounts simultaneously for spatial transport and mass reweighting. We characterize regular barycentric logarithms through optimal semicouplings and measurable selections at the transport threshold, and prove their tangency at arbitrary finite source measures. The defining expansion extends to non-optimal semicouplings, with remainder of smaller order than the square root of their cost. This yields differentiation formulas for simultaneous transport and reweighting and uniqueness of the gradients. We also give a sufficient criterion in terms of regular flat derivatives. We characterize differentiability of one half the squared WFR distance by a common optimal Monge transport--growth representation with no target mass created from the cone vertex. Equivalently, the regular barycentric logarithm is unique and its norm equals the distance; the gradient is minus this logarithm. Finally, we formulate the corresponding calculus on probability measures. On $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, WFR differentiability implies intrinsic Wasserstein differentiability, with the transport component of the WFR gradient coinciding with the Wasserstein gradient. Whenever a flat derivative exists, one quarter of the reaction component agrees almost everywhere with its centered representative. As a byproduct we obtain a Wasserstein differentiability result for the squared $\mathrm{WFR}$ distance.
item.dc:creator: Enrico Sartor

item.title: Row-sparse ah-symmetric reflexive generalized inverses with a few extra rows: local search with approximation guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2611.09719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a rank-$r$ matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, ah-symmetric reflexive generalized inverses $H$ with few nonzero rows give least-squares solutions that are fast to evaluate and use few variables. A known determinant-based local search finds one with exactly $r$ nonzero rows and 2,1-norm within an essentially tight factor $r$ of the minimum at an exact local optimum. We let the nonzero rows of $H$ lie in a set $K$ of $k\ge r$ indices and study how to choose $K$. We bound the loss of this restriction (restricted over unrestricted minimum 2,1-norm) by a simple geometric certificate and establish that a local search maximizing the squared rank-$r$ volume of the corresponding columns of $A$ gives loss at most $\sqrt{k(r+\epsilon k)/(k-r+1)}$, where $1+\epsilon$ is the swap tolerance. With $\epsilon=0$ this is $r$ at $k=r$ and less than $\sqrt{2r}$ for $k\ge2r$; with $\epsilon=1/k$ the search runs in polynomial time on rational data. The same support yields an ah-symmetric reflexive generalized inverse with spectral norm within a factor $\sqrt{1+(n-k)(r+\epsilon k)/(k-r+1)}$ of that of the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. The loss guarantees hold for every norm on the rows. In general, our certificate bound is tight up to a factor depending only on $k/r$, and on some instances, for a suitable row norm, so is the loss bound; for the 2,1-norm, however, the certificate can overestimate the loss by a factor $\sqrt r$. The local search is the Fedorov exchange algorithm of 0/1 D-optimal design; this yields a fast implementation and, via the Kiefer-Wolfowitz theorem, supports of at most $r(r+1)/2+1$ rows with certificate at most $\sqrt r$, best possible in general. On instances from earlier work, the observed loss is far below the guarantee, and the method matches two ADMM heuristics when few rows are removed and otherwise gives 2,1-norms up to 27% smaller, one to two orders of magnitude faster.
item.dc:creator: Marcia Fampa, Jon Lee

item.title: Attractivity Implies Lyapunov Stability for Multidimensional Fornasini--Marchesini Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.09750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the linear multidimensional Fornasini--Marchesini recurrence with uniformly bounded boundary data prescribed on the open coordinate faces. Attractivity is understood in the sense of Pringsheim convergence, in which all discrete indices tend to infinity. We establish that attractivity alone implies Lyapunov stability, and consequently is equivalent to asymptotic stability, for an arbitrary number of discrete directions. Our proof combines inheritance of attractivity by lower-dimensional subsystems, a Baire-category uniform boundedness argument, and word-sum estimates to control coordinate slabs outside the Pringsheim tail. We use a generalized spectral stability criterion proved in a separate companion preprint, without reproving that criterion here. We also obtain a uniform exponential interior estimate and contrast our boundary/convergence convention with an earlier two-dimensional attractivity theorem.
item.dc:creator: Alain Bourget, Tyler McMillen

item.title: Instantaneous control for stabilization of interacting particle systems: convergence rates and dominant frequencies
item.description: arXiv:2611.09838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a class of Cucker-Smale-type systems with a binary interaction potential subject to an external control input. We apply an instantaneous rolling horizon control (IRHC) feedback to address two different control problems: full set-point stabilization of a spatial configuration with zero velocity and stabilization of the center of mass at a desired position with zero mean velocity using a single external agent. The IRHC feedback has been shown to preserve the port-Hamiltonian structure of the corresponding open-loop systems. We analyze how the control parameters and the time discretization affect convergence rates and oscillation frequencies and compare the IRHC feedback with the corresponding IDA-PBC feedback obtained by omitting an additional correction term. For the reduced center of mass dynamics, we derive explicit predictions for continuous- and discrete-time spectral decay rates and oscillation frequencies and verify these predictions numerically. For the full nonlinear particle system, the controller comparison is done by numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Jannik Happ, Birgit Jacob, Claudia Totzeck

item.title: Geometric Pairwise Classification of Affine Constraints over Ellipsoidal Regions
item.description: arXiv:2611.09860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a deterministic geometric procedure for analysing affine constraints over fixed ellipsoidal regions, motivated by chance-constrained set approximation. Analytical tests classify inequalities as always violated, never violated, or cutting. Pairwise tests determine whether two inequalities can be strictly violated at a common point, yielding a compatibility matrix. The tests follow from quadratic optimisation and the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker conditions, with explicit treatment of tangencies, parallel normals, and degenerate inequalities. The formulation applies in arbitrary finite dimensions and provides geometric information for subsequent bounds on simultaneous sampled violations and safe-region approximation.
item.dc:creator: Igor M. L. Pataro, Martina Mammarella, Fabrizio Dabbene, Teodoro Alamo

item.title: Drift-admissibility via Optimal Transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.08505v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce structure-aware optimal transport diagnostics for assessing whether empirical time-series dynamics are compatible with a prescribed predictable-drift class. Our approach translates a pathwise property of stochastic processes into a finite-dimensional projection problem over empirical transition laws, encoding admissibility as row-wise moment constraints on local couplings and quantifying deviations via a Kullback--Leibler projection gap $G_{\lambda,k}$. This yields both a principled diagnostic and a scalable Bregman--Dykstra algorithm that retains the efficiency of Sinkhorn-type methods while incorporating structural constraints. Calibrated against a Brownian reference null, $G_{\lambda,k}$ separates process classes that are indistinguishable by second-order statistics alone---including fractional Brownian motion and BSS processes sharing identical Hurst indices---without asymptotic resampling or continuous-time recovery. This positions the method as a general tool for structure-aware model validation of sequential data.
item.dc:creator: Abigail Langbridge, Enrico Biffis, Jakub Mare\v{c}ek, Robert Shorten

item.title: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective
item.description: arXiv:2611.08571v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neuronal excitability is a nonlinear phenomenon, and the complexity of spiking experimental traces sometimes looks defeating. The present paper takes the view point that excitability is a neuromodulated property, and aims to demonstrate that the neuromodulation of spiking is amenable to the classical linear analysis tools of control theory. We illustrate the value of linear feedback analysis as an alternative to bifurcation analysis in the simple yet classical example of spiking modulation by the A-type potassium current.
item.dc:creator: Fulvio Forni, Rodolphe Sepulchre

item.title: Entropic Martingale Optimal Transport with Wasserstein Relaxed Marginal Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.08743v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Martingale optimal transport (MOT) is a fundamental framework in robust finance, yet its stability under marginal perturbation no longer holds in high dimensions $d\geq 2$. In this paper, we introduce Wasserstein-relaxed entropic martingale optimal transport (WEMOT), which combines Wasserstein relaxation of the second marginal with entropy regularization. This formulation ensures stability under perturbations of the marginals, thereby facilitating numerical implementation. We establish strong duality and dual attainment for WEMOT, which leads to efficient Sinkhorn-type algorithms. We further prove a convergence rate of WEMOT to MOT as regularization parameters vanish, and also the quantitative stability of WEMOT with respect to marginal perturbations.
item.dc:creator: Haowen Chen, Renyuan Xu, Xin Zhang

item.title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
item.description: arXiv:2611.08775v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a network look stable at every layer and still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a basic stability quantity appearing in optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates. Deep networks naturally admit two such notions, input Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to data perturbations, and parameter Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to weight perturbations. We prove that, for deep networks with normalization layers, with batch normalization as the canonical example, both Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth and hence with parameter dimension, even under strong per-layer norm control such as $\|W_\ell\|_2\le 1$, and already for linear activations. Thus, a mechanism widely used to stabilize training can create severe worst-case instabilities that are invisible locally, i.e., from layerwise norm bounds alone. Parameter-Lipschitz explosion turns Lipschitz-dependent nonsmooth optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds for deep normalized networks, while input-Lipschitz explosion makes worst-case Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates vacuous. The latter also yields a concrete rank-separation mechanism for adversarial vulnerability. The theory predicts that perturbations introducing new singular directions should be amplified much more strongly than perturbations at the same noise level that remain within the input's original singular subspace. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support this prediction, showing that rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than same-subspace perturbations.
item.dc:creator: Ashkan Soleymani, Reyhaneh Hosseinpourkhoshkbari, Hadi Daneshmand, Patrick Jaillet

item.title: Synchronized Optimal Transport Reconstructs Coupled Transcriptomic and Chromatin Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.08853v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Single-cell RNA and ATAC data collected across developmental stages provide time-course snapshots of transcriptional and regulatory states. Since sequencing is destructive, trajectories between these snapshots must be inferred from independently sampled cell populations. Existing approaches typically infer continuous dynamics in a single modality or integrate RNA and ATAC in a shared representation. Here we present Cross-Omics Aligned Trajectory Inference (COATI), which extends unbalanced synchronized dynamical optimal transport to time-dependent cross-modal maps for reconstructing coupled trajectories in distinct RNA and ATAC state spaces. We evaluated COATI on synthetic benchmarks and four developmental datasets using held-out-stage reconstruction and lineage analyses. COATI improved reconstruction of cell populations at held-out stages, including recovery of chromatin-state heterogeneity within cell types, and better preserved developmental lineage relationships. The unbalanced formulation allows the inference of population mass changes, which were shown to associate with DNA-replication programs at early stages and lineage-maturation programs later in development. The coupled trajectories enabled analysis of lineage-specific transcriptional and chromatin changes and their temporal relationships during development. Lineage responses inferred by COATI agreed with independent CRISPR perturbation results, and the inferred regulatory patterns were consistent with independent epigenetic data.
item.dc:creator: Jingfeng Wang, Yanxiang Zhao, Qing Nie, Zixuan Cang

item.title: Supporting Data Center Grid Integration via Co-Optimized Battery Energy Storage Sizing and Capacity Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09001v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interconnecting large data centers can be delayed by grid requirements on demand flexibility, ramping limits, and ride-through performance. This paper proposes an optimization-based framework to size a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) that accelerates data center grid integration by providing BESS capacity required to meet selected flexibility and grid-support requirements. The model co-optimizes BESS power rating and energy capacity while allocating capability across three services: (i) demand response over a specified duration, (ii) mitigation of high-magnitude, high-frequency load fluctuations through reserved active power with zero net state-of-charge change, and (iii) voltage support via reactive power capability at the point of common coupling. Minute-level operational scheduling enforces state-of-charge feasibility and load ramp constraints, and incorporates a controllable queue of delay-insensitive computing tasks to enhance flexibility. A case study using a real data center load profile demonstrates the proposed method and quantifies the BESS power-energy requirements and operational trade-offs needed to satisfy the multi-service constraints, providing practical guidance for interconnection planning and deployment.
item.dc:creator: Wei Wang, Himanshu Sharma, Thiagarajan Ramachandran

item.title: Fair Selection of Generalized Nash Equilibria: A Comparability Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2611.09060v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems model self-interested agents coupled through their costs and shared constraints, and arise throughout control applications that allocate a scarce common resource. Such problems typically admit a continuum of equilibria, so any implementation must \emph{select} one. This selection is not neutral: it decides how the cost of the shared constraint is distributed among the agents, a decision often expected to be fair. The variational GNE (v-GNE), which charges all agents a uniform shadow price, is the conventional choice and is frequently advocated as fair. Through the lens of \emph{comparability} from social choice theory, we show that the GNE set itself requires no inter-agent comparability of costs, whereas the v-GNE implicitly assumes cardinal unit comparability, one of the stronger notions. We then introduce the fair GNE (f-GNE), which selects an equilibrium by explicitly optimizing a fairness metric matched to the comparability at hand, and give constructive routes to compute it for single-constraint and linear-quadratic games. An electric-vehicle charging game serves as a running example throughout this self-contained tutorial.
item.dc:creator: Sophie Hall, Heinrich H. Nax, Saverio Bolognani

item.title: Maximizing Reaction via Spatial Localization: The Reaction-Flux Landscape and Maximizing Sequences
item.description: arXiv:2611.09127v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We continue our study of a PDE-constrained variational model for maximizing the total reaction flux by optimizing the spatial distribution of catalytic materials, such as enzymes. The total amount of enzyme is fixed, and the substrate concentration is governed by a reaction-diffusion equation with prescribed boundary values. We consider both linear and nonlinear Michaelis-Menten reaction kinetics. In previous work, we constructed a maximizing sequence, computed the first and second variations of the reaction functional, and established the nonexistence of local maximizers. Here, we conduct a more comprehensive analysis. We prove that the functional is strictly concave for linear kinetics but need not be concave or convex for nonlinear kinetics. We also show that no critical points exist. We then characterize maximizing sequences and identify all their possible limiting measures. Our analysis reveals the mechanism of reaction maximization through spatial localization: maximizing sequences concentrate enzymes near the portion of the boundary where the substrate concentration is largest. Moreover, the landscape of the functional defining the total reaction differs between the linear and nonlinear cases, a point less emphasized in applications. Consistent with existing biophysical studies, these findings motivate the development and analysis of regularized models.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Yasir Feroz Khan, Bo Li

item.title: Controlled Excitation for Identification of Nonlinear Systems with Saturated Outputs
item.description: arXiv:2611.09188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider nonlinear systems whose measured output is the product of an unknown matrix and a known saturation function of the unmeasured state. Generating excitation that allows the matrix to be recovered from the output is challenging when the dynamics are largely unknown. We exploit saturation to construct this excitation. Under a geometric accessibility condition, we derive explicit open-loop controls that drive the state into regions where the saturation takes prescribed values. For componentwise saturations, this condition holds generically with as few as two independent control directions. The controls require no state measurement and only partial knowledge of the dynamics, with no information on the structure of its nonlinear part. The resulting regressor is known in advance, and the unknown matrix is recovered exactly by a closed-form regression. Under stronger structural assumptions and with sufficiently many independent outputs, an output feedback tracks prescribed reference trajectories within the unsaturated region to arbitrary accuracy and permits exact state recovery. Suitably chosen references then also enable exact identification of linearly parameterized (nonlinear) dynamics. We analyze robustness to measurement noise and illustrate the method numerically in the presence of both measurement and dynamical noise.
item.dc:creator: Adel Malik Annabi (McTAO, LJAD), Jean-Baptiste Pomet (McTAO), Dario Prandi (L2S, CNRS), Ludovic Sacchelli (McTAO)

item.title: Provable State Estimation with Recurrent Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.09217v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating the state of a dynamical system from observations is a crucial task in robotics and control. Despite their empirical success, recurrent models often lack formal guarantees on convergence and robustness. We bridge this gap by analyzing these architectures from the perspective of nonlinear observer theory. By framing RNNs as a time-discretization of continuous latent dynamical systems (Neural ODEs), we demonstrate that enforcing a contraction condition on the latent flow guarantees the existence of a smooth, injective map of the true physical state into the latent space. We prove that this architecture acts as a tunable observer: by increasing a single scalar gain that scales the latent vector field, the estimation error can be driven to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of zero at an exponentially fast rate. We further establish quantitative bounds on the MLP complexity required to decode this latent state, and extend our formal guarantees to the discrete-time residual RNN implementation. We validate the theory on a real mobile robotic task, where a provably contracting model outperforms a vanilla GRU with substantially more stable training. We also report that unconstrained GRUs converge to contracting dynamics on this task, suggesting that contraction is an emergent property of well-trained sequence models.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Neural Information Processing Systems Foundation, Dec 2026, Paris, France
item.dc:creator: Vincent Andrieu (LAGEPP, CNRS), Pauline Bernard (CAS), Lucas Brivadis (L2S), Laurent Praly, Christian Wolf

item.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Bounds for $\beta$-TSP
item.description: arXiv:2611.09421v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) asks for a minimum-length Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. Its approximability depends on the edge lengths: unrestricted instances admit no constant-factor approximation unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, metric instances admit Christofides' $3/2$-approximation, and fixed-dimensional Euclidean instances admit a PTAS. We study $\beta$-TSP, where the edge lengths satisfy $ \ell_{uw}\leq\beta(\ell_{uv}+\ell_{vw}) \qquad \forall\,u,v,w\in V\ \text{pairwise distinct}, \quad \beta\in\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]. $ The condition arises naturally in various settings, for example, when metric travel times are combined with positive service times at the vertices. The previous best approximation algorithm, due to B\"ockenhauer et al., ranges from $1$ at $\beta=1/2$ to $3/2$ as $\beta$ approaches $1$. We obtain a strictly better guarantee for every $1/2<\beta<1$ by combining two simple constructions whose guarantees counterbalance each other. We also improve the best known approximation hardness bound for every $1/2<\beta<1$.
item.dc:creator: Paul Liu, Jack Spalding-Jamieson, Da Wei Zheng

item.title: The BCC lattice is the optimal 3D lattice quantizer for all $p\geq1$
item.description: arXiv:2611.09523v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For every finite $p\ge1$, the body-centered cubic lattice uniquely minimizes the $p$th moment of the Voronoi cell among three-dimensional lattices of covolume one, up to orthogonal transformations. This proves the Graf--Luschgy conjecture for three-dimensional lattice quantizers (\cite{GL}).
item.dc:creator: Senping Luo

item.title: Solver-Free Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Edge Selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.09560v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decision-focused learning trains prediction models to improve downstream decisions, but many methods require costly solver calls or optimal-solution labels. We propose a solver-free decision-focused learning framework for NP-hard edge-selection problems with uncertain parameters in the objective, the constraints, or both. A neural optimization layer is first trained without solution labels, using problem objectives and constraint penalties. Graph-informed edge scoring and iterative refinement encourage concentrated and structurally consistent continuous decisions. The layer is then frozen, and a prediction model is trained through its continuous output using a problem-specific loss evaluated under observed parameters. At deployment, the predictor, optimization layer, and a lightweight decoder produce decisions without solving the original NP-hard problem. Experiments on the asymmetric traveling salesperson and endpoint-free orienteering problems show consistently better decision quality than prediction-focused learning and improvements over most evaluated decision-focused baselines. Our framework requires less training time than the evaluated decision-focused baselines, even when optimization-layer pretraining is included. Neural deployment also produces decisions faster than solver-based deployment, offering a better quality-efficiency trade-off. The layer also reduces training cost in existing decision-focused methods when used as an approximate optimization oracle.
item.dc:creator: Xinda Zheng, Frits de Nijs, Edward Lam

item.title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2611.09723v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.
item.dc:creator: Vitalii Aksenov, Sebastian Gutierrez Hernandez

item.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs
item.description: arXiv:2611.09778v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $\rho>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $\rho$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Dobson, Varun Jog, Chun Hei Michael Shiu

item.title: On the (non-)closedness of the set of ReLU networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.09887v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that the set $\mathcal{N}_N$ of ReLU networks with one hidden layer and at most $N\in\mathbb N$ neurons is weakly closed in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, for a bounded connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$. Consequently, every coercive, weakly lower semicontinuous energy on this space attains its minimum over $\mathcal{N}_N$. This covers the Deep Ritz method with convex integrands, Sobolev training and Lipschitz learning. Moreover, as the weight decay parameter tends to zero, minimizers of the regularized problem converge, up to subsequences, to minimizers with minimal parameter norm. We also prove that the set of ReLU networks with two hidden layers of bounded widths is not closed in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ or in $C(\overline\Omega)$. This disproves a conjecture of Petersen, Raslan and Voigtlaender.
item.dc:creator: Eloi Martinet, Leon Bungert

item.title: Integer matrices that are not copositive have certificates of less than quadratic complexity
item.description: arXiv:1306.3867v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A real symmetric matrix is called copositive if the corresponding quadratic form is non-negative on the closed first orthant. If the matrix fails to be copositive there exists some non-negative certificate for which the quadratic form is negative. Due to the scaling property, we can find such certificates in every neighborhood of the origin but their properties depend on the matrix of course and are hard to describe. If it is an integer matrix however, we are guaranteed certificates of a complexity that is at most a constant times the binary encoding length of the matrix raised to the power 3/2.
item.dc:creator: Timo Vilkas

item.title: Best-Worst Disaggregation: An approach to the preference disaggregation problem
item.description: arXiv:2410.12678v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces the Best-Worst Disaggregation (BWD) method, a novel approach that integrates the principles of the Best-Worst Method (BWM) into the disaggregation framework to enhance the consistency and reliability of derived preference models. An optimization model is formulated to determine the most suitable additive value function that fits the preferences expressed by a decision-maker or expert. The method incorporates a consistency analysis to quantify and improve the reliability of the judgments and is extended to handle interval-valued preferences. We also developed an approach to identify a reference set, which is used for pairwise comparisons to elicit the value functions and weights. A case study in logistics performance evaluation demonstrates the practicality and effectiveness of BWD. By coupling a structured human-elicitation protocol with an inference engine and a consistency-feedback loop, BWD provides a human-centered building block for evidence-sensitive decision-support systems
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man and Cybernetics: Systems (2026), 56(11), 7308--7321
item.dc:creator: Matteo Brunelli, Fuqi Liang, Jafar Rezaei

item.title: Kernel Metrics and Learning for Borel MDPs: Identifiability and Adaptive Control
item.description: arXiv:2503.11058v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider a Markov decision process with standard Borel spaces and an unknown transition kernel under the average cost criterion. We do not impose any parametrization on the set of possible kernels. To facilitate our analysis, we first develop implication relations between several topologies on kernels defined by pointwise, continuous, or uniform weak convergence; we then review robustness properties on the space of kernels, and finally we establish compactness conditions on the space of kernels. Building on this regularity analysis, we then present two data-driven identifiability results; the first one being Bayesian and the second one empirical. Our conditions for the Bayesian setting are significantly more relaxed compared with prior work which considered either finite or parametric models, though we do not obtain a rate of convergence. Our analysis is asymptotic and builds on measurability in terms of the tail $\sigma$-field of the available information. Identifiability results are then used to design near-optimal adaptive control policies which alternate between periods of exploration, where the controller acts according to a policy which is conducive to the identification of the true kernel, and periods of exploitation where the controller's information on the kernel is utilized. We will establish that such policies are near optimal. In summary, our contribution is with regard to the general standard Borel setup where there is no apriori parametric representation.
item.dc:creator: Omar Mrani-Zentar, Serdar Y\"uksel

item.title: Differentiable Nonlinear Model Predictive Control
item.description: arXiv:2505.01353v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The efficient computation of parametric solution sensitivities is a key challenge in the integration of learning-enhanced methods with nonlinear model predictive control, as their availability is crucial for many learning algorithms. This paper discusses the computation of solution sensitivities of general nonlinear programs using the implicit function theorem and smoothed optimality conditions treated in interior-point methods (IPM). We introduce sequential barrier quadratic programming (SBQP), which generalizes SQP with an IPM quadratic programming (QP) solver by allowing the barrier parameter to approach a prescribed nonnegative target value, recovering classical SQP when this target is zero. Previous works are limited to convex or unconstrained formulations, or lack an implementation for efficient sensitivity evaluation. The publication is accompanied by an efficient open-source implementation within the `acados` framework, providing both forward and adjoint sensitivities for general optimal control problems, achieving speedups exceeding 3x over the state-of-the-art solvers `mpc.pytorch` and `cvxpygen`.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Frey, Katrin Baumg\"artner, Gianluca Frison, Dirk Reinhardt, Jasper Hoffmann, Leonard Fichtner, Sebastien Gros, Moritz Diehl

item.title: Decentralized Estimation and Control for Leader-Follower Networked Systems with Asymmetric Information Structure
item.description: arXiv:2509.15467v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, the decentralized estimation and linear quadratic (LQ) control problem for a leader-follower networked system (LFNS) is studied from the perspective of asymmetric information. Specifically, for a leader-follower network, the follower agent will be affected by the leader agent, while the follower agent will not affect the leader agent. Hence, the information sets accessed by the control variables of the leader agent and the follower agent are asymmetric, which will bring essential difficulties in finding the optimal control strategy. To this end, the orthogonal decomposition method is adopted to achieve the main results. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: Firstly, the optimal iterative estimation is derived using the conditional independence property established in this paper. Secondly, the optimal decentralized control strategy is derived by decoupling the forward-backward stochastic difference equations (FBSDEs), based on the derived optimal iterative estimation. Thirdly, the necessary and sufficient conditions for the feedback stabilization of the LFNS in infinite-horizon are derived. Finally, the proposed theoretical results are applied to solve the decentralized control problem of a leader-follower autonomous underwater vehicle (LF-AUV) system. The optimal control inputs for the AUVs are provided, and simulation results verify the effectiveness of the obtained results.
item.dc:creator: Yiting Luo, Wei Wang, Qingyuan Qi

item.title: Data-Driven Continuous-Time LQR: Linking Reinforcement Learning and Behavioral System Theory
item.description: arXiv:2604.27922v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Behavioral system theory and reinforcement learning (RL) have independently developed data-driven approaches to the continuous-time LQR problem, yet their respective methods have largely evolved in separation. We connect these two adjacent lines of work by studying their data-driven parameterizations, namely a closed-loop (CL) parameterization from behavioral system theory and an integral RL (IRL) parameterization. The CL parameterization characterizes the closed-loop system via a matrix that satisfies equality constraints. While this parameterization has been extensively studied for discrete-time systems, we adapt key results to the continuous-time setting and develop a policy iteration (PI) scheme, derive an algebraic Riccati equation, and introduce an alternative convex program. The IRL parameterization utilizes off-policy data to perform policy evaluation, which is used for PI or value iteration. Within the IRL framework, we derive a policy gradient flow and propose convex programs for the LQR problem. Finally, we provide a unified treatment of these parameterizations that enables a systematic understanding of existing approaches, and clarifies their structural relationships.
item.dc:creator: Armin Gie{\ss}ler, Felix Th\"ommes, S\"oren Hohmann

item.title: A Measure-Theoretic Formulation of Behavioral Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.01558v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensemble control specifies probability laws on admissible trajectories, including their temporal dependence. Starting from an arbitrary closed behavior, we organize its laws into a framework that connects standard probability-measure geometry, occupation-measure control, and data-driven trajectory parametrization. Classical convexity and extreme-point properties describe the feasible laws, while classical Bellman duality governs additive control objectives. On compact state and input spaces, full-path constrained duality for continuous trajectory functions gives primal attainment and zero gap whenever feasible. For controllable linear time-invariant systems, the noise-free Fundamental Lemma yields an equivalent law-level Hankel factorization, with a canonical pseudoinverse lift. The factorization transfers trajectory-law constraints exactly to coefficient space and connects them to covariance control. Explicit noisy-Hankel bounds quantify subspace approximation for second-moment-bounded laws under known rank and Gaussian output measurement noise. Numerical studies include a nonlinear reset problem whose nonadjacent correlation constraint requires temporal memory, covariance-constrained optimization, and noisy-data policy evaluation. Known transition kernels provide a further structural perspective through history-conditional consistency.
item.dc:creator: Victor M. Preciado

item.title: Implementation-Based Incentive Design for Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand and Transit Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.18687v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Achieving a socially desirable operating point for a multimodal transportation system is challenging when Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) and Public Transit (PT) operators pursue selfish objectives alongside endogenous passenger choices. Existing equilibrium-based regulation models typically search over municipal policies to predict the induced operator equilibrium, creating strong behavioral assumptions, equilibrium-selection issues, and difficult bilevel optimization problems. This paper proposes an implementation-based alternative. Rather than asking which municipal action induces the best equilibrium, we ask: given a target operating profile, what minimum realized transfer makes unilateral deviation unattractive for each operator? Using k-implementation theory, this payment decomposes into two unilateral deviation gains: one for the AMoD operator and one for PT. Calculating this payment requires computing three distinct objects: the social target, the AMoD best response, and the PT best response. This is nontrivial because each represents a large-scale network optimization problem complicated by endogenous mode choice and congestion. To address this, we develop tailored mathematical formulations and algorithms for each oracle. For the social target, we derive a decomposition and entropy-regularized mixed-integer convex formulation balancing social optimality and implementability. For the AMoD oracle, we derive an exact reformulation, a convex relaxation providing a global upper bound, and a sequential convex approximation for feasible lower bounds. For the PT oracle, we develop a mixed-integer convex relaxation and characterize its exactness condition. A NYC case study shows the framework computes tight implementation-payment bounds and reveals how the dominant source of incentive misalignment shifts with congestion.
item.dc:creator: Xinling Li, Runyu Zhang, Gioele Zardini

item.title: Optimal Oracle Complexity for Weakly Convex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2608.03246v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the oracle complexity of finding $\epsilon$-stationary points of $\rho$-weakly convex and $G$-Lipschitz functions, where stationarity is measured by the gradient of the Moreau envelope. We consider an exact first-order oracle that returns both the function value and the full subdifferential at every query point. In the principal parameter regime, we prove that every first-order algorithm, including randomized algorithms, requires $\Omega(\tfrac{\rho G^2\Delta}{\epsilon^4})$ oracle queries to succeed with any fixed positive probability, where $f(0)-\inf f\le\Delta$. This lower bound matches the best known deterministic and stochastic first-order upper bounds, up to universal constants, and establishes the optimal randomized first-order oracle complexity. The result separates smooth nonconvex and weakly convex optimization: the additional $\epsilon^{-2}$ factor is intrinsic to nonsmooth geometry rather than stochastic oracle noise.
item.dc:creator: Jiajin Li, Siyu Pan

item.title: Amortized Score-Hamiltonian Policy Iteration: A Grid-Free Scheme for Relaxed Stochastic Control Problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.04285v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop an amortized, grid-free implementation of continuous Langevin dynamics based policy-value iteration for entropy-regularized, infinite-horizon relaxed stochastic control problems. The improvement rate of the exact iteration is a discounted aggregate of relative Fisher information between the policy and the Gibbs law of its Hamiltonian. The associated score residual is the velocity with which the control's Langevin dynamics transport its law. We project this velocity onto a conditional sampler shared across states, instead of one Langevin dynamics per state, and the value dynamics onto a parametric critic, estimating both projections at sampled states to obtain coupled actor--critic flows. The score loss measures the actor's agreement with the current critic, while the policy-evaluation residual measures the critic's agreement with the actor. We also derive gradient and Hessian residuals, including a Feynman--Kac representation for the gradient equation, to control errors not detected by the projected value iteration. An exact decomposition of the HJB residual combines these errors into a policy-suboptimality bound under verification and logarithmic Sobolev assumptions. In the linear-quadratic class, both projections are exact and recover the pointwise iteration, and we provide numerical experiments on general models to demonstrate the coupled actor--critic learning in high-dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Qi Feng, Gu Wang

item.title: Adaptive Variance Reduction across Smoothness and Noise Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2610.13799v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study adaptive stochastic non-convex optimization under unknown smoothness and noise conditions. Our algorithms require no smoothness constant, noise bound, initial function gap, or oracle-regime label. We first propose a fixed-budget method that combines normalized momentum, recursive variance reduction, and a fresh gradient stage, followed by fresh validation of the candidates. We prove that the same output has expected gradient norm $O(T^{-1/4})$ under objective smoothness and bounded noise variance, $O(T^{-1/3})$ under average smoothness, and $O(T^{-1/2})$ for noiseless gradients, where $T$ counts individual gradient evaluations. We then develop an anytime algorithm whose three optimization paths preserve their endpoints across reporting and budget-extension boundaries. The same three rates hold at every deterministic query budget, although the algorithm receives no information about the budget $T$. The analysis combines a scale potential, a uniform second-moment bound, and accounting for candidates retained through unfinished blocks. An optional sample-mean selector further reduces cumulative validation work from $O(T)$ to $O(T^{2/3})$ while preserving these rates.
item.dc:creator: Wei Jiang, Yibo Wang, Sifan Yang, Lijun Zhang, Zechao Li

item.title: Descending Everest, Part I: Oracle Complexity of Convex Optimization under $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness
item.description: arXiv:2610.21461v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions, the curvature may grow together with the gradient norm. Therefore, even when $\|x^0-x^*\|\le R$, the gradient and the optimality gap at the starting point may be exponentially large in $L_1R$, and the bound $\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}$, known for the accelerated method on functions with Lipschitz gradient, no longer describes the complexity of the problem. We determine the oracle complexity of this class for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods: for $L_0R^2/\varepsilon\ge1$, the optimal number of oracle calls $N$ satisfies $1+N=\widetilde\Theta(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+L_1R)$. The upper bound reads $O(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+(1+L_1R)\log(2+L_1R))$: the method first passes through the large-gradient regime in $O(1+L_1R)$ iterations with an inexact line search, and then the standard accelerated method with a constant stepsize takes over. The lower bound is obtained by means of chains and the orthogonal invariance principle on functions conjugate to strongly convex functions on a polytope. If the initial optimality gap is at most $4\varepsilon$, the optimal bound becomes $1+N=\widetilde\Theta(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+(L_1R)^{2/3})$.
item.dc:creator: Mikhail Rudomanov, Ivan Fomin, Alexander V. Gasnikov, Fedor S. Stonyakin

item.title: Defense Filters for Robust Learning of Partially Observed Dynamical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.21935v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robust estimation of unknown system dynamics from partial observations under attack is a core challenge in learning for control, increasingly critical in multi-agent networks subject to adversarial data poisoning. Existing methods either require highly restrictive assumptions on the adversary or yield weak error bounds. In this paper, we consider identifying partially observed linear dynamical systems subject to adversarial attacks with an attack probability $p < 0.5$ at each time. We propose a defense-filtering framework leveraging knowledge of the observation matrix to construct a defense filter satisfying full column rank and subspace separability conditions, which enables the evaluation of a single-attack scenario against observed data. Using this framework, we analyze the constrained $\ell_2$-norm estimator and establish finite-sample error bounds for recovering the Markov parameter matrix up to a linear transformation. This is the first approach to provide provable system identification guarantees via a defense filter for partially observed systems subject to harsh environments where the attack probability approaches $0.5$.
item.dc:creator: Jihun Kim, Javad Lavaei

item.title: Descending Everest, Part II: Oracle Complexity of Minimizing a Sum of Convex $(L_0,L_1)$-Smooth Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.04171v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the minimization of the average of $n$ convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions: the Hessian norm of each function is bounded by an affine function of its gradient norm. We assume known upper bounds $R$ on the distance from the starting point to a minimizer and $\delta$ on the difference between the minimum of the average and the average of the infima of the components. We derive upper and lower bounds on the oracle complexity of reaching accuracy $\varepsilon$ in function value in expectation. Up to logarithmic factors, both bounds are of order $n(1+(L_1R)^{2/3}) +\sqrt{\frac{n(L_0+L_1^2\delta)R^2}{\varepsilon}+n(L_1R)^2}$. The upper bound is attained by the proposed method YETI. The method combines ideas of accelerated proximal methods and variance reduction methods with a heuristic for choosing additional points. The number of oracle calls made by the heuristic is bounded, which preserves the upper bound on the total number of queries needed to reach the target accuracy. In the experiments, YETI is compared with first-order methods on synthetic problems and Poisson regression problems. We also examine the stopping criterion and the effect of the heuristic separately. The lower bound is obtained by an explicit construction of families of instances that are hard for any first-order method.
item.dc:creator: Mikhail Rudomanov, Ivan Fomin, Alexander V. Gasnikov, Fedor S. Stonyakin

item.title: Convergence of optimizers implies eigenvalues filtering at equilibrium
item.description: arXiv:2510.09034v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ample empirical evidence in deep neural network training suggests that a variety of optimizers tend to find nearly global optima. In this article, we adopt the reversed perspective that convergence to an arbitrary point is assumed rather than proven, focusing on the consequences of this assumption. From this viewpoint, in line with recent advances on the edge-of-stability phenomenon, we argue that different optimizers effectively act as eigenvalue filters determined by their hyperparameters. Specifically, the standard gradient descent method inherently avoids the sharpest minima, whereas Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) algorithms go even further by actively favoring wider basins. Inspired by these insights, we propose two novel algorithms that exhibit enhanced eigenvalue filtering, effectively promoting wider minima. Our theoretical analysis leverages a generalized Hadamard--Perron stable manifold theorem and applies to general semialgebraic $C^2$ functions, without requiring additional non-degeneracy conditions or global Lipschitz bound assumptions. We support our conclusions with numerical experiments on feed-forward neural networks.
